1. Loot all the things... Take a companion to help carry all the items you collect; many of the junk items will be useful at some point for crafting. You can tag specific items so that a little magnifying glass icon appears when you look at them. In the armor or weapon crafting station, if you don't have the required items, you can push the designated button (I'm playing on a console, not sure about the controls for other systems, but it should indicate at the bottom of the screen) to tag all the items you need.

2. Don't rush the main quest. I've only had this game for about 2 weeks, so I'm not 100% sure if this is true for this particular title, but my experience with other games from the same developer is that if you rush the main quest, you'll finish it pretty quickly and probably won't even see a quarter of the map. Take your time, explore, read terminals, and listen to audio logs you find; nearly every location has a little backstory to learn about and items to discover.

3. Pick one type of weapon to invest perks in and stick to it for a good while. For example, there's a perk to increase damage with single-shot rifles, single-shot pistols, or automatic weapons, etc. Decide which one you want to use and focus on that type for a while so you can save perk points for other things. Also, carry several weapons of that type that use different ammunition. For instance, if you choose single-shot rifles, you can carry a shotgun, a pipe or combat rifle, and a laser rifle, as long as it doesn't have an automatic modification. This way, you should have some decent weapons available, so if you run out of ammo for one, you have backups.

4. The further away from your starting area you get, the more dangerous things become. Take care when exploring; if you are unsure, then quick save. Be prepared to run away (having a companion can help with this because they can't die and will usually keep fighting, which can buy you time to escape).

When I was in my early 20s, I used to have really bad insomnia; I could easily still be up at 4 a.m. and not feel tired at all. Anyway, one night, it must have been 1 or 2 a.m., I was sitting at the computer looking online, trying to get sleepy when there was a knock at the door. It was pretty unusual to get someone at the door at that time, but I figured maybe it was an emergency from one of my neighbors (on one side, there was a house where several individuals with disabilities lived with a caregiver, so I thought I should answer just in case).

So, I answered the door, and there was a random girl I had never met and didn’t recognize at all. She was dressed in everyday clothes, not like someone who had been out partying—just jeans and a hoodie—and didn’t seem to be intoxicated in any way. She said she was told there was a party at my house, but I told her there wasn’t; it was just me home alone trying to get tired enough to sleep. She then asked if she could use my phone. Always wanting to believe the best in people (before real adult cynicism set in), I invited her in and showed her to the phone. She kind of dialed numbers (which looked more like she pushed numbers at random) and waited for someone to answer (note: I have no idea if she actually called someone or if it was an act).

After about 10 minutes of this, she gave up and claimed she was actually homeless. Now, not to stereotype or anything, but her appearance didn’t suggest she’d been sleeping rough at all; her clothing was casual but not grubby, frayed, or worn out in any way, so I was kind of suspicious. I Googled the nearest shelter, and there was one about a mile away, certainly within walking distance, so I agreed to walk her there (it was the middle of the night, after all).

On the walk, she started trying to hold my hand, stroke my arm, that kind of thing, until we got to the end of the street where the shelter was. Single-player games generally have a limited replay value; players typically experience them once or a few times before moving on. Even with added DLC, players might revisit the game briefly but will likely set it aside again. In contrast, online games tend to have a much longer lifespan, especially with regular updates, particularly when those updates are free. By concentrating their resources on enhancing the online experience, developers can ensure ongoing sales for the game. Even without additional purchases, this approach is often the more lucrative option if they are willing to continue supporting it. To put it another way, there's a reason this game is the best-selling entertainment title ever, and it's not solely due to the single-player mode.
